english_translation: Take this cup and put it near the window before you go out.

dialogue.shona: Tora kapu iyi uiise pedyo nefafitera usati wabuda.
dialogue.english: Take this cup and put it near the window before you go out.
dialogue.literal_gloss: Tora [take! / pick up!] • kapu [cup] • iyi [iyi] • uiise [uiise] • pedyo [pedyo] • nefafitera [and / with fafitera] • usati [usati] • wabuda [wabuda]

grammar_notes.title: Giving Commands & Polite Requests ('Tora')
grammar_notes.content: Notice the command verb 'Tora' in this sentence. In Shona, a direct command to one person (singular) is simply the verb stem ending in '-a'—for example, 'Vhara!' ('Close!'), 'Tora!' ('Take!'), or 'Huya!' ('Come!'). When speaking to more than one person, or when showing polite respect to an adult, you add '-i' to the end, changing '-a' to '-ai' (as in 'Huyai!' = 'Come!' or 'Batai!' = 'Catch/Hold!'). Adding the prefix 'chi-' (as in 'Chiuya' or 'Chigara') means 'Do it right now'.
grammar_notes.rule: Singular Command: Verb stem (-a) [Huya! / Tora!] | Polite or Plural Command: Verb stem + -i (-ai) [Huyai! / Torai!]

grammar_notes.title: Talking About Location: 'pa-', 'ku-', and 'mu-' ('pedyo')
grammar_notes.content:
Look at how location is expressed with 'pedyo'. Instead of separate prepositions like 'on', 'to', or 'in', Shona attaches one of three location prefixes directly to the front of a noun:
• 'pa-' means 'at' or 'on' a specific point or surface (e.g., 'patafura' = on the table, 'pamusika' = at the market, 'pasi' = on the ground).
• 'ku-' means 'to', 'from', or 'at' a general destination (e.g., 'kuchikoro' = to school, 'kumusha' = to the rural home, 'kubasa' = at/to work).
• 'mu-' means 'inside' an enclosed space (e.g., 'mumba' = inside the house, 'muguta' = in the city, 'mumugwagwa' = in the road).
grammar_notes.rule: pa- = on / at a point (patafura) | ku- = to / at a place (kuchikoro) | mu- = inside (mumba)

grammar_notes.title: Saying 'If', 'When', and 'Before' ('kana' & '-sati')
grammar_notes.content: To link two events in time or condition, Shona uses 'kana' ('if / when'). When talking about a future condition ('If we work hard...'), the verb after 'kana' takes '-ka-' (e.g., 'kana tikashanda' = 'if we work'). When 'kana' sits between two nouns (like 'tsvuku kana nhema'), it simply means 'or'! To say 'before' something happens, Shona uses '-sati' ('not yet') followed by a past-form verb: 'usati wabuda' ('before you go out') or 'tisati tadya' ('before we eat').
grammar_notes.rule: kana = if / when / or | [ndisati / usati / tisati] + past verb = before [I / you / we] do something

cultural_notes.title: Morning Tea, Bread & Hospitality at Home
cultural_notes.content: Breakfast in many Zimbabwean households centres around hot tea with milk ('mukaka') and sugar ('shuga') served alongside fresh bread ('chingwa') or home-grown sweet potatoes and groundnut butter. When a visitor arrives at any time of day, offering a cup ('kapu') of tea or cool drinking water ('mvura') at the table ('patafura') is an essential expression of household hospitality.

active_exercises.prompt: How do you politely ask someone to speak softly ('taura zvinyoronyoro')?
In 'Uya kuno undibatsire', what does the prefix '-ndi-' inside 'undibatsire' mean?
active_exercises.explanation: The object prefix '-ndi-' always means 'me', placed directly before the verb stem '-batsira' (help).

active_exercises.prompt: If a friend asks you in the afternoon 'Waswera sei?', what is the natural reply?
active_exercises.explanation: In Shona, you reply to 'Waswera sei?' ('How did you spend the day?') with 'Ndaswera kana waswerawo' ('I spent the day well if you spent it well too').
